props.title: L'Argent
props.initialSlug: A counterfeit note sparks a tragic moral downfall

sections.content: Robert Bresson's final film **L'Argent** (1983) represents the culmination of his austere filmmaking style, tracing how a counterfeit 500-franc note triggers a devastating chain of moral corruption. Building on themes from his earlier works like Pickpocket (1959) and **A Man Escaped** (1956), Bresson strips away conventional dramatic elements to expose the mechanical nature of modern society. The film's clinical precision mirrors earlier French classics like **Army of Shadows** (1969), but Bresson pushes further into spiritual desolation.

sections.content: Bresson's "model" system of using non-professional actors reaches its apex in **L'Argent**, with performances stripped of theatrical expression. This approach influenced later minimalist directors like Bruno Dumont in **L'Humanité** (1999) and the Dardenne brothers with **Rosetta** (1999). The film's stark examination of money's corrupting influence echoes through contemporary works like **A Prophet** (2009) and **Capital** (2012), though few match Bresson's radical formal restraint.

The film's rigorous framing and precise sound design established a template for what critics would later call "transcendental style," influencing directors like Paul Schrader, whose **First Reformed** (2017) directly channels Bresson's aesthetic. The mechanical repetition of gestures and focus on hands and objects rather than faces became a signature of European art cinema, seen in works like Michael Haneke's **The White Ribbon** (2009). sections.content: While **L'Argent**'s commercial failure marked the end of Bresson's career, its influence continues to reverberate. The film's unflinching examination of moral corruption through economic systems influenced works like **The Wolf of Wall Street** (2013) and **Parasite** (2019), though these films employ more conventional narrative approaches. The stark photography and emphasis on material details finds echoes in Kelly Reichardt's **Wendy and Lucy** (2008) and the Safdie brothers' **Good Time** (2017).
